segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Meanwhile Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and asked him for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any who belonged to the Way, men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was traveling and getting near Damascus, suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and falling to the ground he heard a voice saying to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Who are you, Lord?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he replied,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But get up and go into the city, and you will be told what you must do.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The men who were traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Saul got up from the ground, but though his eyes were open he could see nothing. So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For three days he could not see, and he neither ate nor drank.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now there was a disciple in Damascus named Ananias, and the Lord said to him in a vision,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Ananias.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Here I am, Lord.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Lord said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Get up and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man from Tarsus named Saul. For look, he is praying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he may see again.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Ananias answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, I have heard from many people about this man, how much harm he has done to your holy ones in Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the Lord said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go, for this man is my chosen instrument to carry my name before Gentiles and kings and the sons of Israel.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For I myself will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Ananias went and entered the house. He laid his hands on him and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Brother Saul, the Lord has sent me—Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you were coming here—so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he could see again. He got up and was baptized,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and after taking food he regained his strength. He spent some days with the disciples in Damascus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At once he began proclaiming Jesus in the synagogues: that he is the Son of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: All who heard him were astonished and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Isn’t this the man who wreaked havoc in Jerusalem on those who call on this name? And hadn’t he come here for this very purpose, to bring them bound before the chief priests?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Saul grew all the more powerful and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus, proving that Jesus is the Messiah.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When many days had passed, the Jews plotted together to kill him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but their plot became known to Saul. They were even watching the gates day and night in order to kill him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but his disciples took him by night and let him down through the wall, lowering him in a basket.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he arrived in Jerusalem, he tried to join the disciples, but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles, and he related to them how on the road Saul had seen the Lord, and that the Lord had spoken to him, and how in Damascus he had spoken boldly in the name of Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he was with them, going in and out in Jerusalem, speaking boldly in the name of the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He also spoke and debated with the Hellenists, but they were trying to kill him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the brothers learned of this, they took him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the assembly throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up; and walking in the fear of the Lord and in the encouragement of the Holy Spirit, it grew in numbers.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now as Peter was traveling through all those places, he came down also to the holy ones who lived in Lydda.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There he found a man named Aeneas, who had been lying on a mat for eight years; he was paralyzed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Get up and make your bed.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And immediately he got up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: All who lived in Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha, which translated is Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity, which she was always doing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In those days she became ill and died. They washed her and laid her in an upstairs room.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, urging him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do not delay in coming to us.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Peter got up and went with them. When he arrived, they took him up to the upstairs room, and all the widows stood beside him, weeping and showing the tunics and cloaks that Dorcas used to make while she was with them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Peter put them all outside, knelt down, and prayed. Then, turning to the body, he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Tabitha, get up.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She opened her eyes, and seeing Peter she sat up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He gave her his hand and raised her up. Then he called the holy ones and the widows and presented her alive.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Peter stayed for many days in Joppa with a certain Simon, a tanner.

notes.note: Acts uses “the Way” as a name for the movement of Jesus’s followers (also 19:9, 19:23, 22:4, 24:14, 24:22). The Greek word is the ordinary one for a road or path, and it is the same word translated “road” in verses 17 and 27.

The Greek form of address ranges from a polite “sir” to “Lord” as a divine title. Saul does not yet know who is speaking, so “sir” is possible, but a voice from heaven in a blaze of light calls for more than courtesy. Most translations therefore keep “Lord,” as here.

The Greek word means both “voice” and “sound.” In Paul’s retelling at Acts 22:9 his companions saw the light but did not hear the voice of the one speaking to him. Many interpreters reconcile the two accounts by taking this verse to mean they heard a sound without making out words; others think Luke simply varied the details. “Voice” is kept because it is the same word as in verse 4.

The traditional rendering is “saints,” which now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The word is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people” or “his holy people.”

One Greek word means both “nations” and, in the plural, the non-Jewish peoples. Here it stands alongside “the sons of Israel,” so “Gentiles” is the sense, as in most translations. Elsewhere in this translation the same word appears as “nation” or “nations” where peoples as such are meant.

The traditional rendering is “the Christ.” Here the word is a title under argument in the synagogues—whether Jesus is the anointed king Israel expected—and “Messiah” conveys that to a modern reader. Where the word works as part of a name, as in “Jesus Christ” in verse 34, “Christ” is kept; several modern translations make the same split.

The earliest manuscripts read “his disciples,” implying that Saul already had followers of his own in Damascus. Many later manuscripts read “the disciples took him,” and some scholars suspect the earlier reading arose from a copying slip. The translation follows the earlier reading.

Most likely Greek-speaking Jews, many of them from the diaspora but living in Jerusalem, as distinct from the Aramaic-speaking “Hebrews” of Acts 6:1. Saul, himself a Greek-speaking Jew from Tarsus, debates his own circle—the circle that had earlier opposed Stephen (6:9).

The traditional rendering is “church,” which is near-universal but now suggests a building or an institution. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Septuagint’s term for Israel assembled, and “assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word stays visible. The singular here, covering believers in three regions, is the reading of the earliest manuscripts; later ones have the plural.

The Greek is literally “spread for yourself,” with no object stated. The usual understanding is the spreading of bedding, so “make your bed.” The same verb can be used of preparing a couch for a meal, so a minority take it as “get yourself something to eat.”
Tabitha is Aramaic and Dorcas is Greek; both mean “gazelle.” Luke gives the Greek equivalent for his readers, and she was probably known by both names in the mixed-language port of Joppa.

Tanners worked with animal carcasses, and the trade was foul-smelling and looked down on; later rabbinic sources treat it as a despised occupation. Peter’s lodging with a tanner sets the scene for the next chapter, where the question of clean and unclean comes to a head.

candidates.reason: As a term for fellow believers it recurs throughout Acts and the letters, and translators split between “brothers,” “brothers and sisters” and “believers.”
As Acts’ name for the movement it needs one capitalized rendering, kept distinct from the ordinary “road” or “way.”
Translations vary between “comfort,” “encouragement,” “consolation” and “exhortation” across Luke–Acts, Paul and Hebrews, which hides that it is one word.
“Preach” and “proclaim” are both common, and the word is frequent enough across the Gospels, Acts and the letters to need one choice.
It occurs only in Acts 6:1, 9:29 and possibly 11:20, and “Hellenists,” “Greek-speaking Jews” and “Hellenistic Jews” are all in use, so it should be fixed once.

Verse 26: πειράζω is not rendered with a register form (test; tempt; tempter; put to the test; examine; try / attempt) and has no register-exception note.
